options.a: Orders and reviews the appraisal, then sets the final loan amount the lender will approve
options.b: Performs clerical loan processing such as gathering documents for a licensed originator
options.c: Takes a residential mortgage application and/or offers/negotiates terms for compensation
options.d: Makes the final credit decision and issues the commitment letter for the lender

distractorExplanations.a: Ordering appraisals and setting the final amount are processing/underwriting functions; SAFE Act MLO activity is taking applications and offering or negotiating terms.
distractorExplanations.b: Clerical or support processing under a licensed MLO's supervision is excluded from the SAFE Act MLO definition; the MLO takes applications and negotiates terms.
distractorExplanations.d: Final credit decisions and commitment letters are underwriting functions; an MLO is defined by taking applications and offering/negotiating terms for pay.

options.a: Monthly debt obligations to net take-home pay
options.b: Total outstanding debt balances to annual income
options.c: Loan amount to the property's appraised value
options.d: Monthly debt obligations to gross monthly income

distractorExplanations.a: DTI uses gross (pre-tax) monthly income, not net take-home pay; using net income would overstate the ratio.
distractorExplanations.b: DTI compares monthly payments, not total outstanding balances, to monthly income; balance-to-income is a different measure.
distractorExplanations.c: Loan amount divided by appraised value is the loan-to-value (LTV) ratio, a collateral measure rather than a capacity measure like DTI.

options.a: Principal, interest, title, and inspection
options.b: Points, interest, taxes, and insurance
options.c: Principal, interest, taxes, and insurance
options.d: Principal, interest, and transfer taxes

distractorExplanations.a: Title and inspection are one-time closing costs; the T and I in PITI stand for property taxes and hazard insurance paid monthly.
distractorExplanations.b: The P in PITI is principal, not discount points; points are a one-time upfront charge, not part of the monthly housing payment.
distractorExplanations.d: Transfer taxes are a one-time closing charge; PITI includes recurring property taxes plus homeowners insurance.

options.a: Exit the contract if the home appraises below the purchase price
options.b: Exit the contract if the home inspection reveals material defects
options.c: Exit or renegotiate if they cannot obtain specified financing
options.d: Exit if they cannot sell their current home before closing

distractorExplanations.a: Exiting on a low value is an appraisal contingency; a financing contingency covers failure to obtain the specified loan.
distractorExplanations.b: Defect findings trigger an inspection contingency, not a financing contingency, which hinges on obtaining the specified loan.
distractorExplanations.d: Making the purchase depend on selling the buyer's existing home is a home-sale contingency, not a financing contingency.

options.a: Evaluate credit, capacity, collateral, and compliance risk against guidelines
options.b: Take the application and negotiate rate and terms with the borrower
options.c: Collect documents, order verifications, and prepare the file for review
options.d: Coordinate the closing, disburse loan funds, and record the security instrument

distractorExplanations.b: Taking applications and negotiating terms is the loan originator's role; the underwriter independently evaluates risk against guidelines.
distractorExplanations.c: Gathering documents and ordering verifications is the processor's job; the underwriter decides whether the file meets guidelines.
distractorExplanations.d: Disbursing funds and recording documents are closing/settlement agent tasks, not the underwriter's risk evaluation.

options.a: Commits the lender to approve the loan at the quoted rate once the lock is signed
options.b: Holds the quoted rate until closing, however long the transaction takes
options.c: Fixes the rate for the first five years before adjustments begin on an ARM
options.d: Protects the quoted interest rate for a stated period if conditions are met

distractorExplanations.a: A lock protects pricing only; it is not a credit approval, and the loan still has to clear underwriting before closing.
distractorExplanations.b: Locks expire after a stated period (e.g., 30-60 days); delays past expiration can require an extension fee or repricing.
distractorExplanations.c: That describes an ARM's initial fixed period in the note, not a pre-closing rate lock that protects quoted pricing until closing.

options.a: All monthly debts including housing relative to income
options.b: Non-housing installment debts relative to income
options.c: Housing payment relative to the property's value
options.d: Housing payment (often PITI) relative to income

distractorExplanations.a: Including every monthly debt plus housing describes the back-end ratio; the front-end ratio isolates the housing payment.
distractorExplanations.b: Non-housing installment debts are part of the back-end calculation, not the front-end housing ratio.
distractorExplanations.c: Front-end DTI divides housing expense by gross income, not property value; payment-to-value is not a standard qualifying ratio.

options.a: An informal estimate based on borrower-stated income and assets without verification
options.b: A final loan commitment issued after the appraisal and title are approved
options.c: A more verified underwriting review of credit/income/assets
options.d: A rate lock on the program the borrower selects before choosing a specific property

distractorExplanations.a: Unverified, borrower-stated estimates describe pre-qualification; pre-approval involves a credit pull and document verification.
distractorExplanations.b: A final commitment comes after appraisal, title, and conditions clear; pre-approval precedes a property and is not a commitment.
distractorExplanations.d: A rate lock protects pricing on a specific loan; pre-approval is a verified credit review, not a pricing lock.

options.a: Intends to occupy the property for part of the year
options.b: Intends to rent the property while living elsewhere
options.c: Intends to occupy the property as their main home
options.d: Lists it as a mailing address while living in another home

distractorExplanations.a: Part-year occupancy describes a second home; a primary residence is the borrower's principal, main home.
distractorExplanations.b: Renting the property out while living elsewhere makes it an investment property, not a primary residence.
distractorExplanations.d: A mailing address alone does not establish occupancy; the borrower must actually live in the home as their principal residence.

options.a: A gift letter alone, since the donor's statement is sufficient proof
options.b: Proof the funds sat in the borrower's account for 60 days before closing
options.c: A promissory note showing repayment terms agreed with the donor
options.d: A gift letter and evidence of transfer/sourcing per program rules

distractorExplanations.a: A gift letter by itself is not enough; lenders also require evidence of the donor's transfer and sourcing of the funds.
distractorExplanations.b: Seasoning funds for 60 days is a way to avoid sourcing; gift funds instead require a gift letter and documentation of the transfer.
distractorExplanations.c: A repayment obligation turns the gift into a loan that must be counted in DTI; a true gift requires no repayment.

options.a: A loan amount above FHA county loan limits
options.b: A loan amount above conforming loan limits
options.c: A loan with an LTV ratio above 95 percent
options.d: A loan secured by a two- to four-unit property

distractorExplanations.a: FHA limits cap FHA eligibility; a jumbo is defined by exceeding the conforming limit set for Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac.
distractorExplanations.c: A high LTV describes leverage, not loan size; jumbo status depends on the loan amount exceeding conforming limits.
distractorExplanations.d: Two- to four-unit properties have their own higher conforming limits; unit count alone does not make a loan jumbo.

options.a: A single inquiry for scoring purposes under common scoring model rules
options.b: Separate inquiries, each lowering the score by a fixed number of points
options.c: Soft inquiries that do not appear on the consumer's credit report
options.d: A single inquiry only if every pull comes from the same lender

distractorExplanations.b: Scoring models deduplicate mortgage inquiries within a shopping window rather than penalizing each pull separately.
distractorExplanations.c: Mortgage pulls are hard inquiries and do appear on the report; the window only collapses them into one for scoring.
distractorExplanations.d: Rate-shopping windows apply across different lenders; the point is to let consumers compare lenders without score penalties.

options.a: The loan has funded and the deed of trust has been recorded
options.b: The underwriter issued approval subject to remaining conditions
options.c: Underwriting conditions are satisfied
options.d: The title company has cleared all liens so the seller may be paid

distractorExplanations.a: Funding and recording happen after closing; clear-to-close is the earlier signal that underwriting conditions are satisfied.
distractorExplanations.b: Approval subject to conditions is conditional approval; clear-to-close means those conditions have already been satisfied.
distractorExplanations.d: Clearing title is one input; clear-to-close is the lender's underwriting sign-off that every loan condition is satisfied.

mortgage-loan-originator-readiness-check.explanation: CTC indicates underwriting conditions are met and the loan may proceed to closing (final walk-through/funding still matter).

options.a: Insured by the Federal Housing Administration, often allowing lower down payments
options.b: Backed by a VA guaranty for eligible veterans, often with no down payment
options.c: Purchased by Fannie Mae under conforming guidelines with a low down payment
options.d: Funded directly by HUD for first-time buyers whose incomes fall below area median limits

distractorExplanations.b: A VA guaranty for eligible veterans describes VA loans; FHA loans are insured by the Federal Housing Administration.
distractorExplanations.c: Fannie Mae buys conventional conforming loans; FHA loans are government-insured and typically securitized through Ginnie Mae.
distractorExplanations.d: FHA does not lend directly or impose income caps; approved lenders make the loans and FHA insures them.

options.a: The total monthly payment including escrow constant for the loan's life
options.b: The interest rate constant until the first scheduled adjustment date
options.c: The interest rate constant for the life of the loan
options.d: The principal balance constant until the loan reaches maturity

distractorExplanations.a: Only the note rate and P&I are fixed; escrowed taxes and insurance can change, so the total payment may change.
distractorExplanations.b: Scheduled adjustment dates belong to ARMs; a fixed-rate mortgage has no rate adjustment during the loan term.
distractorExplanations.d: That describes an interest-only or balloon structure; a fixed-rate amortizing loan reduces principal each month.

mortgage-loan-originator-readiness-check.explanation: Fixed-rate locks the note rate; PITI can change if taxes/insurance change, so the payment may still change with escrow.

options.a: Can adjust based on the margin alone, which resets at each adjustment
options.b: Can adjust based on an index plus margin after an initial fixed period
options.c: Can adjust based on the lender's prime rate at its sole discretion
options.d: Can adjust based on the borrower's credit score at each anniversary

distractorExplanations.a: The margin is fixed for the life of an ARM; it is the index that moves, and the rate equals index plus margin.
distractorExplanations.c: ARM changes follow a published, independent index plus a margin set in the note, not a rate the lender controls.
distractorExplanations.d: Credit score affects initial pricing; ARM adjustments follow the index plus margin, not changes in the borrower's credit.

options.a: Eligible veterans buying in rural areas with no income or geographic limits
options.b: Eligible borrowers in qualifying rural/suburban areas meeting income limits
options.c: First-time buyers in any area with incomes above the area median
options.d: Farmers financing agricultural land and equipment for commercial use

distractorExplanations.a: Veteran status is the VA program's test; USDA eligibility turns on property location and household income limits.
distractorExplanations.c: USDA requires an eligible rural/suburban location and caps income (typically 115% of area median) rather than requiring above-median income.
distractorExplanations.d: Farm-operating credit is a separate USDA Farm Service Agency program; the rural housing loan finances primary residences.

options.a: Require interest plus a small principal amount on a 40-year schedule
options.b: Require payments below accrued interest, so the balance grows
options.c: Require level principal-and-interest payments based on a fixed rate
options.d: Require payment of interest only, so principal may not decline

distractorExplanations.a: Paying principal on a longer schedule is extended amortization; during the IO period no principal payment is required.
distractorExplanations.b: Paying less than accrued interest is negative amortization; IO payments cover the full interest so the balance stays level.
distractorExplanations.c: Level P&I payments describe a fully amortizing fixed-rate loan; during the IO period the payment covers interest alone.

options.a: A revolving line of credit secured by home equity
options.b: A closed-end second mortgage paid out in one lump sum
options.c: A reverse mortgage line drawn by borrowers age 62+
options.d: An unsecured personal line of credit for home repairs

distractorExplanations.b: A lump-sum, closed-end second lien is a home equity loan; a HELOC is a revolving line the borrower draws on as needed.
distractorExplanations.c: A HECM line of credit is a reverse mortgage with no required monthly payments; a HELOC is a forward revolving line that must be repaid.
distractorExplanations.d: A HELOC is secured by a lien on the home's equity; an unsecured line carries no collateral and is a different product.

options.a: A payment that rises at each adjustment as the index increases
options.b: Payments that start low and rise by a set percentage each year
options.c: Interest-only payments that convert to amortizing payments after ten years
options.d: A large principal balance due at a stated maturity before full amortization

distractorExplanations.a: Payment increases tied to an index describe an ARM; a balloon is a lump-sum balance due before the loan fully amortizes.
distractorExplanations.b: Scheduled annual payment increases describe a graduated payment mortgage, not a balloon's lump sum at maturity.
distractorExplanations.c: Converting to amortizing payments after the IO period still pays the loan off over the term; a balloon leaves a large balance due early.

options.a: Mortgage insurance coverage required based on FICO and LTV
options.b: Pricing/cost based on risk factors like FICO, LTV, product type
options.c: The maximum loan amount allowed based on FICO and LTV
options.d: Underwriting approval decisions based on FICO, LTV, and DTI

distractorExplanations.a: MI coverage levels are set by investor/MI rules; LLPAs are Fannie/Freddie price adjustments charged for risk attributes.
distractorExplanations.c: Maximum loan amounts come from conforming limits and program caps; LLPAs change pricing, not the loan limit.
distractorExplanations.d: Approve/refer decisions come from AUS and underwriting; LLPAs affect the price of a loan that is already eligible.

options.a: Finance the land purchase, with building funded separately
options.b: Finance building then convert to a permanent mortgage
options.c: Finance repairs to an existing home bought in one loan
options.d: Provide short-term funds to buy before selling the old home

distractorExplanations.a: A lot/land loan finances the land; a construction-to-perm loan funds building and rolls into the long-term mortgage.
distractorExplanations.c: Combining purchase with repairs on an existing home describes a renovation loan such as FHA 203(k), not new construction.
distractorExplanations.d: Short-term financing to buy before selling is a bridge loan; construction-to-perm converts building financing into a mortgage.

options.a: Payments cover interest only, so the principal balance stays level
options.b: Rising property values reduce the loan-to-value ratio over time
options.c: Payments are insufficient to cover accruing interest, so balance rises
options.d: Extra principal payments shorten the loan term below the schedule

distractorExplanations.a: Paying exactly the interest keeps principal flat (interest-only); negative amortization requires paying less than the interest due.
distractorExplanations.b: Appreciation lowers LTV but does not change the loan balance; negative amortization is about unpaid interest added to principal.
distractorExplanations.d: Extra principal accelerates amortization, the opposite of negative amortization where the balance grows.

options.a: Disclosure timing rules for the Loan Estimate and Closing Disclosure under TRID
options.b: Fair lending standards prohibiting discrimination on protected bases under ECOA
options.c: Underwriting standards designed to assess ability to repay under ATR/QM framework
options.d: Eligibility standards for conventional loans that Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac may purchase

distractorExplanations.a: LE/CD timing is TRID (Reg Z 1026.19); QM/ATR governs whether the creditor reasonably determined repayment ability.
distractorExplanations.b: Prohibited-basis discrimination is ECOA/Reg B; QM is part of the Reg Z ability-to-repay underwriting framework.
distractorExplanations.d: GSE purchase eligibility is set by agency selling guides; QM is a CFPB ATR standard that applies to creditors generally.

options.a: A federal tax credit related to mortgage interest for eligible borrowers
options.b: A federal tax deduction for all mortgage interest paid by any homeowner
options.c: A state grant that covers the down payment for first-time buyers
options.d: A certificate that exempts eligible borrowers from mortgage insurance

distractorExplanations.b: The mortgage interest deduction is a separate itemized deduction; an MCC is a dollar-for-dollar credit for eligible (often first-time) buyers.
distractorExplanations.c: Down payment assistance grants are separate programs; an MCC converts part of the mortgage interest into a federal tax credit.
distractorExplanations.d: MCCs do not affect mortgage insurance requirements; they provide a federal tax credit on a portion of mortgage interest.

options.a: APR disclosure, finance charge accuracy, and rescission rights on refinances
options.b: Collection of loan application data and reporting of lending patterns
options.c: Prohibited bases for credit decisions and the content and timing of adverse action notices
options.d: Settlement costs, servicing disclosures, and prohibitions on kickbacks/unearned fees

distractorExplanations.a: APR, finance charge, and rescission are TILA/Reg Z topics; RESPA/Reg X governs settlement costs, servicing, and kickbacks.
distractorExplanations.b: Application data collection and reporting is HMDA/Reg C; RESPA focuses on settlement costs and anti-kickback rules.
distractorExplanations.c: Prohibited bases and adverse action notices are ECOA/Reg B requirements, not RESPA settlement-procedure rules.

options.a: Settlement service referrals, kickback and unearned fee prohibitions, and escrow account limits
options.b: Licensing standards, background checks, and testing for loan originators
options.c: Truthful disclosure of credit terms/APR and certain advertising/ability-to-repay rules
options.d: Permissible purpose for credit reports and consumer dispute procedures

distractorExplanations.a: Kickback bans and escrow limits are RESPA/Reg X; TILA/Reg Z governs credit-cost disclosure, advertising, and ATR.
distractorExplanations.b: Licensing, background checks, and testing are SAFE Act requirements, not TILA credit-term disclosure rules.
distractorExplanations.d: Permissible purpose and disputes are FCRA topics; TILA covers APR and credit-term disclosures plus ATR and advertising.

options.a: Good Faith Estimate and HUD-1 settlement statement rules
options.b: Adverse action notice and appraisal copy delivery rules
options.c: Loan Estimate and Closing Disclosure timing/content rules
options.d: Initial escrow statement and servicing transfer notice rules

distractorExplanations.a: The GFE and HUD-1 are the pre-2015 RESPA forms that TRID replaced with the Loan Estimate and Closing Disclosure.
distractorExplanations.b: Adverse action notices and appraisal copies are ECOA/Reg B requirements, not part of the TILA-RESPA integrated disclosures.
distractorExplanations.d: Escrow statements and servicing transfer notices remain separate RESPA/Reg X requirements outside the TRID LE/CD forms.

options.a: Protected characteristics such as race, color, religion, national origin, sex, marital status, and age
options.b: Characteristics such as race, color, religion, national origin, sex, handicap, and familial status
options.c: Characteristics such as race, color, religion, sex, and national origin, but not age or marital status
options.d: Characteristics such as occupation, length of employment, credit history, and property location

distractorExplanations.b: Handicap and familial status are Fair Housing Act bases; ECOA adds marital status, age, and receipt of public assistance instead.
distractorExplanations.c: ECOA expressly covers marital status and age (with limited exceptions); excluding them confuses ECOA with a shorter civil-rights list.
distractorExplanations.d: Occupation, job tenure, and credit history are permissible underwriting factors, not ECOA prohibited bases.

mortgage-loan-originator-readiness-check.explanation: ECOA bars credit discrimination on listed prohibited bases, including age (with limits), receipt of public assistance, and good-faith exercise of consumer credit rights.

options.a: Race, color, religion, sex, marital status, age, and receipt of public assistance
options.b: Race, color, religion, sex, handicap, familial status, national origin
options.c: Race, color, religion, sex, and national origin, but not familial status
options.d: Race, color, national origin, income level, and credit history

distractorExplanations.a: Marital status, age, and public assistance are ECOA bases; the Fair Housing Act adds handicap and familial status instead.
distractorExplanations.c: Familial status (households with children under 18) was added to the Fair Housing Act by the 1988 amendments and is protected.
distractorExplanations.d: Income level and credit history are not Fair Housing Act protected classes; they are legitimate underwriting factors.

options.a: Provide adverse action notices on denied loans
options.b: Meet the credit needs of their local communities
options.c: Deliver Loan Estimates within three business days
options.d: Report specified mortgage application/loan data

distractorExplanations.a: Adverse action notices are an ECOA/Reg B requirement; HMDA requires collecting and reporting application and loan data.
distractorExplanations.b: Serving local community credit needs is the Community Reinvestment Act's mandate; HMDA is a data reporting law.
distractorExplanations.c: Loan Estimate timing comes from TRID under Reg Z; HMDA (Reg C) concerns reporting application and loan data.

options.a: Be licensed only by the federal CFPB, with states having no licensing role
options.b: Be registered with HUD and complete FHA lender approval before originating
options.c: Be licensed/registered via NMLS as applicable and meet education/testing standards
options.d: Complete testing once, with no ongoing education after licensure is granted

distractorExplanations.a: States license MLOs under SAFE Act standards; federal registration through NMLS applies to depository-institution employees.
distractorExplanations.b: HUD/FHA approval applies to lenders for FHA programs; SAFE Act licensing/registration of individuals runs through NMLS.
distractorExplanations.d: SAFE Act licensees must complete at least 8 hours of approved continuing education every year to renew.

options.a: Verify customer identity under a written CIP
options.b: File suspicious activity reports on fraud
options.c: Have a written identity theft prevention program
options.d: Provide annual privacy notices to customers

distractorExplanations.a: A Customer Identification Program is a BSA/USA PATRIOT Act requirement; the Red Flags Rule requires an identity theft prevention program.
distractorExplanations.b: SAR filing is a Bank Secrecy Act/AML obligation; the FACTA Red Flags Rule requires a written identity theft program.
distractorExplanations.d: Annual privacy notices are a GLBA Privacy Rule requirement, not part of the Red Flags identity theft prevention program.

options.a: Within 3 business days of application (TRID timing)
options.b: Within 7 business days of application (TRID timing)
options.c: Within 10 business days of application (TRID timing)
options.d: Within 30 days of application (TRID timing)

distractorExplanations.b: Seven business days is the waiting period between LE delivery and consummation, not the deadline to issue the LE.
distractorExplanations.c: Ten business days is the minimum period the LE's estimated charges must stay available, not the delivery deadline.
distractorExplanations.d: Thirty days is the Reg B deadline to notify an applicant of action taken on a completed application, not the LE deadline.

options.a: At least 1 business day before consummation, as with the old HUD-1 review
options.b: At least 3 business days before consummation (with limited exceptions)
options.c: At least 7 business days before consummation (with limited exceptions)
options.d: At consummation, when the consumer signs the note and security instrument

distractorExplanations.a: One business day was the HUD-1 inspection right under pre-TRID RESPA; TRID requires CD receipt three business days before consummation.
distractorExplanations.c: Seven business days is the LE waiting period before consummation; the CD must be received three business days before.
distractorExplanations.d: Delivering the CD at the closing table violates TRID; the consumer must receive it at least three business days before consummation.

options.a: RESPA Section 8, which bans payments made by borrowers to their MLO
options.b: TILA anti-steering/LO compensation rules and fair dealing standards
options.c: HMDA reporting rules, which bar reporting loans with higher pricing
options.d: The SAFE Act, which caps MLO commissions at a percentage of the loan

distractorExplanations.a: Section 8 targets referral kickbacks and unearned fees among settlement providers; steering for compensation is a Reg Z LO comp issue.
distractorExplanations.c: HMDA requires reporting pricing data rather than restricting it; anti-steering is a TILA/Reg Z LO compensation rule.
distractorExplanations.d: The SAFE Act sets licensing standards and does not cap commissions; compensation-based steering falls under TILA LO comp rules.

options.a: An interior appraisal ordered by the MLO, who may discuss target values
options.b: An automated valuation model accepted in place of a full interior inspection
options.c: Compliance with appraisal independence and HPML appraisal rules where applicable
options.d: A second appraisal on every refinance, paid for by the consumer

distractorExplanations.a: Appraisal independence bars originators from influencing or suggesting values; HPML rules add a written interior appraisal requirement.
distractorExplanations.b: HPML appraisal rules require a written appraisal with an interior inspection by a certified or licensed appraiser, not an AVM.
distractorExplanations.d: A second appraisal applies to certain HPML flips (resale within 180 days at a markup) and cannot be charged to the consumer.

options.a: The property is in a moderate-risk Zone X area and the borrower has filed no prior flood insurance claims
options.b: The property is in a Special Flood Hazard Area, but only when the loan is FHA or VA
options.c: The flood zone determination is pending and the loan amount exceeds the county limit
options.d: The property is in a Special Flood Hazard Area and the loan is secured by that improved real estate

distractorExplanations.a: Zone X is outside the Special Flood Hazard Area; mandatory purchase applies to SFHA zones such as A and V.
distractorExplanations.b: Mandatory flood insurance applies to loans from federally regulated lenders and GSE-purchased loans, not just FHA/VA loans.
distractorExplanations.c: The trigger is an SFHA determination on improved property, not loan size; a pending determination must be completed before closing.

mortgage-loan-originator-readiness-check.explanation: Mandatory flood insurance applies to SFHA properties with designated loans from a regulated lender (or loans the GSEs buy).

options.a: A permissible fee if disclosed on the Loan Estimate
options.b: A TILA finance charge violation subject to rescission
options.c: An unearned fee / potential RESPA Section 8 violation
options.d: A zero-tolerance violation curable by a lender credit

distractorExplanations.a: Disclosure does not cure an unearned fee; RESPA Section 8(b) bars charges for which no service is actually performed.
distractorExplanations.b: Finance-charge errors can trigger TILA remedies, but charging for no service is the RESPA Section 8 unearned-fee problem.
distractorExplanations.d: TRID tolerance cures address fee increases over the LE; they do not legitimize a fee for which no service was performed.

options.a: A permissible lender-credit structure
options.b: Deceptive advertising / UDAAP risk
options.c: A RESPA Section 8 kickback violation
options.d: A TRID 10% tolerance violation

distractorExplanations.a: Lender credits can be legitimate, but advertising 'no closing costs' while hiding the cost in the rate is deceptive.
distractorExplanations.c: Section 8 covers referral kickbacks between settlement providers; misleading cost claims are a deceptive advertising/UDAAP issue.
distractorExplanations.d: Tolerance buckets limit fee increases from the LE; a misleading 'no closing cost' claim is an advertising/UDAAP problem.

options.a: Restricted/prohibited under LO compensation rules
options.b: Permitted if both payments are disclosed on the CD
options.c: Permitted when the borrower requests it in writing
options.d: A RESPA Section 8 violation curable by refund

distractorExplanations.b: Disclosure does not cure dual compensation; Reg Z bars receiving both consumer- and creditor-paid comp on the same loan.
distractorExplanations.c: A borrower request does not allow dual compensation; the LO comp rule restricts it under Reg Z even with consent.
distractorExplanations.d: Dual compensation is governed by TILA's LO compensation rule, not RESPA Section 8, and is not cured by a refund.

options.a: Address it; do not submit known false information
options.b: Submit it and let the underwriter decide if it matters
options.c: Have the borrower initial the change at closing
options.d: Wait to see whether the AUS flags it before acting

distractorExplanations.b: Knowingly passing false data to underwriting makes the MLO complicit in fraud; the MLO must address it before submission.
distractorExplanations.c: Initialing a misstatement at closing does not correct it; the MLO must fix the record before the file goes to underwriting.
distractorExplanations.d: Waiting for the AUS to catch a known misstatement is willful blindness; the MLO must address it and not submit false data.

options.a: A referral is made to an affiliate settlement provider
options.b: A lender pays a broker yield spread on a loan
options.c: A borrower chooses an unaffiliated title company
options.d: A servicer transfers servicing rights to another firm

distractorExplanations.b: Lender-paid broker compensation is an LO comp/TILA disclosure matter, not an affiliated business arrangement referral.
distractorExplanations.c: AfBA disclosure is triggered by referrals to providers with an ownership affiliation, not by an unaffiliated choice.
distractorExplanations.d: Servicing transfers require a RESPA servicing transfer notice, not an affiliated business arrangement disclosure.

options.a: Permitted if the APR is shown in the ad's fine print
options.b: Acceptable if the rate was available for one borrower
options.c: Unethical and potentially illegal deceptive advertising
options.d: A RESPA Section 8 violation for unearned referral fees

distractorExplanations.a: Including an APR does not cure advertising a rate that is not actually available; the ad remains deceptive.
distractorExplanations.b: Advertised rates must be reasonably available to qualified consumers; one isolated borrower does not make a teaser honest.
distractorExplanations.d: Section 8 targets kickbacks and unearned fees; bait-and-switch rate advertising is deceptive advertising under TILA/UDAAP.

options.a: HMDA data confidentiality and reporting rules
options.b: FCRA permissible purpose rules for credit reports
options.c: GLBA privacy/safeguards expectations and ethics
options.d: RESPA Section 8 rules on settlement referrals

distractorExplanations.a: HMDA governs reporting of application data; protecting borrower NPI from unauthorized use is a GLBA matter.
distractorExplanations.b: FCRA permissible purpose limits credit report pulls; using a borrower's NPI for personal marketing falls under GLBA privacy rules.
distractorExplanations.d: Section 8 concerns kickbacks for settlement referrals, not unauthorized use of a borrower's nonpublic personal information.

options.a: RESPA allows splits only with licensed real estate agents
options.b: Licensing/SAFE Act and compensation rules may be violated
options.c: The fee must be disclosed as a finance charge on the LE
options.d: HMDA requires reporting the unlicensed person's NMLS ID

distractorExplanations.a: RESPA Section 8 does not authorize referral splits with agents; the issue here is paying an unlicensed person for MLO activity.
distractorExplanations.c: Disclosure classification is not the problem; paying an unlicensed person to take applications violates SAFE Act licensing.
distractorExplanations.d: An unlicensed person has no NMLS ID; the core problem is compensating unlicensed MLO activity under the SAFE Act.

options.a: A buyer inflating income on the application to qualify for a larger loan
options.b: An appraiser inflating the value so a seller can pay off an underwater loan
options.c: A seller paying the buyer's down payment through an undisclosed side agreement
options.d: Someone posing as the buyer to obtain a loan for another party, often fraudulently

distractorExplanations.a: Inflating income is income fraud by the actual borrower; a straw buyer lends their name and credit for someone else.
distractorExplanations.b: Inflated valuations describe appraisal/property flipping fraud; a straw buyer is a stand-in borrower for a hidden party.
distractorExplanations.c: Undisclosed seller-funded down payments are down payment fraud, not a stand-in borrower scheme.

options.a: Unfair, discriminatory, or abusive acts or practices
options.b: Unlawful disclosure and appraisal practices
options.c: Unfair, deceptive, or abusive acts or practices
options.d: Unfair or deceptive acts or practices (FTC Act)

distractorExplanations.a: The D stands for deceptive, not discriminatory; discrimination is addressed separately under ECOA and the Fair Housing Act.
distractorExplanations.b: UDAAP is not about disclosures or appraisals specifically; it stands for unfair, deceptive, or abusive acts or practices.
distractorExplanations.d: Unfair or deceptive (UDAP) is the FTC Act standard; Dodd-Frank added 'abusive' to create the CFPB's UDAAP standard.

options.a: Borrower credit scores, the appraised value, and the final approved loan terms issued by underwriting
options.b: Settlement charges, cash to close, and closing cost details disclosed to the borrower
options.c: Demographic data only, used by the lender for HMDA government monitoring reporting
options.d: Borrower identity, income, assets, liabilities, and property/transaction details for underwriting

distractorExplanations.a: Credit scores, appraisal results, and final terms come from third-party reports and underwriting, not from the 1003 application.
distractorExplanations.b: Settlement charges and cash to close are disclosed on the Loan Estimate and Closing Disclosure, not collected on the URLA.
distractorExplanations.c: The URLA includes a demographic section for HMDA, but its main purpose is collecting identity, income, assets, and liabilities.

options.a: Cancel or renegotiate without penalty if mortgage approval is not obtained by the deadline
options.b: Cancel without penalty if the property appraises below the agreed purchase price
options.c: Cancel without penalty if the inspection reveals defects the seller refuses to repair before closing
options.d: Cancel without penalty if the buyer cannot sell their current home by the deadline

distractorExplanations.b: A low appraisal triggers an appraisal contingency; a financing contingency turns on failing to get loan approval.
distractorExplanations.c: Unrepaired defects are covered by an inspection contingency, not the financing contingency.
distractorExplanations.d: Dependence on selling an existing home is a home-sale contingency, distinct from obtaining mortgage approval.

options.a: Boundary lines, encroachments, and lot dimensions from a physical survey
options.b: Recorded liens, easements, and ownership claims affecting the property
options.c: Structural defects, code violations, and needed repairs at the property
options.d: Flood zone status and hazard insurance requirements for the property

distractorExplanations.a: Boundary lines and encroachments are found by a survey; a title search reviews recorded liens, easements, and ownership.
distractorExplanations.c: Physical defects and code issues are found by a home inspection, not a search of public title records.
distractorExplanations.d: Flood zone status comes from a flood determination using FEMA maps, not from the title search of recorded documents.

options.a: Holds the buyer's earnest money deposit until the purchase contract closes
options.b: Collects a full year of taxes and insurance at closing, with no monthly deposits after
options.c: Collects monthly portions of annual tax and insurance bills paid by the servicer when due
options.d: Collects monthly amounts the servicer may hold with no cushion limit under RESPA

distractorExplanations.a: Earnest money is held in a purchase escrow by a title/escrow agent; an impound account pays taxes and insurance after closing.
distractorExplanations.b: Closing funds an initial deposit and cushion, but the borrower then pays monthly escrow installments with each payment.
distractorExplanations.d: RESPA limits the escrow cushion to one-sixth (two months) of annual disbursements and requires an annual analysis.

options.a: The loan is cleared to close, pending only the borrower's signature at closing
options.b: The underwriter has suspended the file because key information cannot be verified as submitted
options.c: The borrower is pre-approved but has not yet identified a property to purchase
options.d: The underwriter needs additional documents or clearances before issuing final approval

distractorExplanations.a: Clear-to-close comes after conditions are satisfied; conditional approval means items are still outstanding.
distractorExplanations.b: A suspense status halts review until missing information arrives; conditional approval is a yes subject to listed items.
distractorExplanations.c: Pre-approval precedes a property contract; conditional approval is an underwriting decision on a specific loan file.

options.a: Evaluate risk and eligibility using investor guidelines and submitted application data
options.b: Issue a final credit decision that the underwriter cannot override or condition
options.c: Generate the Loan Estimate and calculate tolerance cures for the closing
options.d: Verify the borrower's identity against OFAC and fraud databases before application

distractorExplanations.b: AUS findings are recommendations; underwriters validate data, add conditions, and may decline despite an approve finding.
distractorExplanations.c: LE generation and tolerance cures happen in the LOS/disclosure system; AUS evaluates risk and eligibility.
distractorExplanations.d: OFAC and fraud screening are separate compliance tools; DU and LP assess credit risk and program eligibility.

options.a: A letter from the borrower promising to pay the account off within 30 days after the closing date
options.b: Verification the account will be paid from closing proceeds and will not reappear on credit
options.c: Exclusion of the payment from DTI once the balance falls below ten monthly payments
options.d: Closing of the account by the creditor before the borrower submits the application

distractorExplanations.a: A promise to pay after closing does not remove the debt from DTI; the payoff must be documented at or before closing.
distractorExplanations.c: The 10-month rule applies to installment debts that will run out soon, not to debts being paid off at closing.
distractorExplanations.d: The debt need not be closed before application; it must be shown paid from closing proceeds and documented.

options.a: A verification of rent and 12 months of canceled checks to landlords as proof of reserves
options.b: Year-end account statements from the prior tax year showing average balances
options.c: Recent bank/investment statements, large deposit sourcing, and gift documentation when applicable
options.d: Current account balances plus the borrower's available credit card limits as reserves

distractorExplanations.a: Rent history shows payment behavior, not liquid funds; reserves are verified with account statements and sourced deposits.
distractorExplanations.b: Lenders want the most recent statements (typically two months), not prior-year balances, plus sourcing of large deposits.
distractorExplanations.d: Unused credit lines are borrowed funds, not reserves; reserves must be verified liquid assets owned by the borrower.

options.a: The borrower's two-year employment history and job title from the original W-2 forms
options.b: The employer's written agreement to deduct mortgage payments directly from the borrower's paycheck
options.c: The borrower's credit report shows no new debts opened since the initial application
options.d: The borrower is still employed with consistent income as represented on the application

distractorExplanations.a: W-2 history is reviewed at application; a pre-closing VOE confirms the borrower is still employed as represented.
distractorExplanations.b: Employers do not set up payroll deductions for mortgages as part of a VOE; it confirms current employment and income.
distractorExplanations.c: Checking for new debts is a credit refresh or undisclosed-debt monitoring, not the verbal or written VOE.

options.a: The principal balance reaches a scheduled LTV threshold under federal homeowner protection rules
options.b: The home's current market value rises enough for the loan-to-value ratio to reach 85 percent
options.c: The borrower requests cancellation once the principal balance reaches 90 percent of the original value
options.d: The borrower has made 24 consecutive on-time payments at any loan-to-value ratio

distractorExplanations.b: Automatic termination follows the amortization schedule against original value at 78%, not appreciation to 85%.
distractorExplanations.c: Borrower-requested cancellation starts at 80% of original value, not 90%; automatic termination occurs at 78%.
distractorExplanations.d: Payment history alone does not end PMI; HPA termination requires reaching the 78% LTV schedule (or the loan midpoint).

mortgage-loan-originator-readiness-check.explanation: Under the Homeowners Protection Act, automatic termination is often at 78% of original value with timely payments. Borrower-initiated cancellation at 80% LTV may also be available with good payment history and no subordinate liens.

options.a: Is excluded from CLTV when the second lien is held by a different lender
options.b: Increases combined loan-to-value and may affect PMI, pricing, and program eligibility
options.c: Lowers the first-lien LTV, so the second lien's payment is excluded from DTI
options.d: Requires the first-lien lender to subordinate its position to the new second lien

distractorExplanations.a: CLTV counts every lien on the property whoever holds it; a separate lender does not remove the second lien from the calculation.
distractorExplanations.c: Although the first-lien LTV may be lower, the second lien's monthly payment must be included in the borrower's DTI.
distractorExplanations.d: On a purchase the first mortgage is recorded first; subordination is needed when refinancing a first while keeping a second.

options.a: The borrower must have held the current rate lock for a minimum period before closing
options.b: The borrower must wait a minimum period after a refinance before applying for a HELOC
options.c: The borrower must have owned the property for a minimum period before tapping equity
options.d: The borrower must have made 36 months of payments before any cash-out is permitted

distractorExplanations.a: Lock duration is a pricing term; cash-out seasoning measures how long the borrower has owned the property or been on title.
distractorExplanations.b: HELOC timing is set by the lender; cash-out seasoning is about ownership time before a cash-out refinance.
distractorExplanations.d: Seasoning is measured mainly by time on title (often 6-12 months), not a 36-month payment count.

mortgage-loan-originator-readiness-check.explanation: Agency guides limit cash-out soon after acquisition to reduce flip and fraud risk; the exact seasoning period varies by agency/investor.

options.a: Must occupy the home within 60 days of closing, the same as the primary borrower
options.b: Is a guarantor who signs the note but whose income cannot be used to qualify
options.c: Holds title to the property but does not sign the note or the mortgage
options.d: May help qualify using income/assets but does not intend to live in the home

distractorExplanations.a: That 60-day move-in describes an occupant borrower's obligation; a non-occupant co-borrower does not live in the home.
distractorExplanations.b: Non-occupant co-borrower income can be used to qualify (subject to program rules); a guarantor-only role is a different concept.
distractorExplanations.c: A titleholder who doesn't sign the note is a non-borrowing title holder; a co-borrower signs the note and is obligated.

options.a: May follow alternative income/asset verification paths but still requires credible repayment analysis
options.b: Must rely on the borrower's stated income, because third-party verification applies only to QM loans
options.c: Requires the creditor to consider the eight ATR factors but without any third-party verification of them
options.d: Follows the same rules as QM but gives the creditor a stronger legal safe harbor

distractorExplanations.b: ATR requires verifying income using reasonably reliable third-party records for every covered mortgage; stated-income lending is not allowed.
distractorExplanations.c: The ATR rule requires both considering the eight factors and verifying them with reasonably reliable third-party records.
distractorExplanations.d: Non-QM loans lack the QM safe harbor or presumption; the creditor bears more litigation risk, not less.

options.a: Permanently lowers the note rate in exchange for discount points the borrower pays at closing
options.b: Lowers the borrower's payment in early years using funds held to subsidize interest
options.c: Lowers the payment in early years by adding the unpaid interest to the balance
options.d: Lowers the rate for the first five years, then adjusts with an index and margin

distractorExplanations.a: Paying discount points for a lower note rate is a permanent buydown; a temporary buydown subsidizes payments for a few years.
distractorExplanations.c: Adding unpaid interest to principal is negative amortization (like a GPM); a buydown uses a funded subsidy account instead.
distractorExplanations.d: Index-plus-margin adjustments after a fixed period describe an ARM; a temporary buydown keeps the note rate and subsidizes payments.

options.a: The maximum loan amount FHA will insure for a one-unit property in a given county
options.b: The maximum loan-to-value ratio Fannie Mae or Freddie Mac allows for a primary residence
options.c: The minimum loan amount a lender must originate to sell the loan to Ginnie Mae
options.d: The maximum loan amount eligible for purchase by Fannie Mae or Freddie Mac in a given area

distractorExplanations.a: FHA sets its own county mortgage limits; conforming limits govern Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac purchases.
distractorExplanations.b: Maximum LTV is an eligibility guideline; the conforming limit is a dollar cap on loan size set annually by FHFA.
distractorExplanations.c: Ginnie Mae guarantees securities backed by government loans and sets no such minimum; conforming limits are maximums.

options.a: Upfront and annual mortgage insurance premiums with lower down payment options for eligible borrowers
options.b: Private mortgage insurance that cancels at 78% LTV, with a 5% minimum down payment
options.c: A one-time funding fee instead of monthly insurance, with no down payment for eligible borrowers
options.d: Income below 115% of area median and a property located in an eligible rural area

distractorExplanations.b: Cancelable PMI and 5% minimums describe conventional loans; FHA uses upfront and annual MIP with a 3.5% minimum down.
distractorExplanations.c: A funding fee with no down payment describes VA loans; FHA charges upfront plus annual mortgage insurance premiums.
distractorExplanations.d: Income caps and rural location are USDA eligibility tests; FHA has no income limit or geographic restriction.

options.a: Is a monthly premium that cancels when the loan reaches 78 percent LTV
options.b: Helps sustain the VA loan program and may be financed into the loan amount
options.c: Must be paid in cash at closing and cannot be added to the loan amount
options.d: Is the same flat amount for every veteran, including those receiving VA disability pay

distractorExplanations.a: VA loans have no monthly mortgage insurance; the funding fee is a one-time charge, and 78% cancellation is a conventional PMI rule.
distractorExplanations.c: The VA funding fee can be financed into the loan; requiring it in cash confuses it with other closing costs.
distractorExplanations.d: The fee varies by down payment, service type, and first vs subsequent use; veterans receiving VA disability compensation are exempt.

options.a: Lower monthly payments and less total interest because the rate is lower
options.b: The same monthly payment but a lower interest rate, so the loan builds equity much faster
options.c: Higher monthly payments but less total interest paid over the life of the loan
options.d: Higher monthly payments and more total interest because of the higher rate

distractorExplanations.a: A lower rate helps, but the shorter term raises the monthly payment; payments are higher, not lower, on a 15-year loan.
distractorExplanations.b: Compressing repayment into 15 years raises the payment even at a lower rate; the payment is not the same.
distractorExplanations.d: 15-year rates are typically lower, and fewer years of interest mean less total interest, not more.

options.a: Borrowers at least age 55 who occupy the home as a principal residence
options.b: Borrowers at least age 62 who may rent the home out as an investment property
options.c: Borrowers of any age who own the home free and clear and live there full time
options.d: Borrowers at least age 62 who occupy the home as a principal residence

distractorExplanations.a: Age 55 is used by some proprietary reverse mortgages; the FHA-insured HECM requires borrowers to be at least 62.
distractorExplanations.b: HECMs require the home to be the borrower's principal residence; investment properties are ineligible.
distractorExplanations.c: HECMs require borrowers to be at least 62, and an existing mortgage may be paid off with proceeds rather than owned free and clear.

mortgage-loan-originator-readiness-check.explanation: HECMs are FHA-insured reverse mortgages with specific counseling and non-recourse features; borrowers must also complete HUD-approved counseling and meet financial assessment tests.

options.a: A fixed rate for five years, then annual adjustments based on an index plus margin
options.b: A fixed rate for one year, then adjustments every five years based on an index
options.c: A fixed rate for five years, then a balloon payment of the remaining balance
options.d: A fixed rate for five years, then rate adjustments every six months based on an index plus margin

distractorExplanations.b: The first number is the initial fixed period (five years) and the second is the adjustment frequency (one year).
distractorExplanations.c: A five-year balloon requires a lump-sum payoff; a 5/1 ARM continues amortizing with annual rate adjustments.
distractorExplanations.d: Six-month adjustments after five years describe a 5/6 ARM (common with SOFR); a 5/1 adjusts annually.

options.a: Finance the purchase of a vacant lot and the construction of a new single-family home
options.b: Finance purchase or refinance plus eligible repair/improvement costs in one loan
options.c: Finance repairs alone, as an unsecured personal loan insured under FHA Title I
options.d: Finance a home that already meets FHA standards, with repairs paid by the seller

distractorExplanations.a: Lot purchase plus new construction is a construction-to-permanent loan; 203(k) rehabilitates an existing dwelling.
distractorExplanations.c: FHA Title I property improvement loans are separate; 203(k) combines purchase/refinance with repair costs in one mortgage.
distractorExplanations.d: Seller-paid repairs before closing are a standard FHA purchase; 203(k) rolls the borrower's repair costs into the loan.

options.a: Is sold to Fannie Mae with servicing retained by the originating lender
options.b: Is securitized through Ginnie Mae as an FHA or VA government loan
options.c: Uses the lender's internal guidelines rather than solely selling to GSEs
options.d: Is exempt from ATR rules because the lender keeps the credit risk

distractorExplanations.a: Selling to Fannie Mae with servicing retained is still a GSE sale; a portfolio loan is held on the lender's own books.
distractorExplanations.b: Ginnie Mae securitization covers government loans sold into MBS; portfolio loans are retained by the lender.
distractorExplanations.d: ATR applies to portfolio loans too; small-creditor portfolio QM offers a compliance path, not an exemption from repayment analysis.

options.a: A first mortgage at 80% LTV, PMI at 10% coverage, and a 10% down payment
options.b: A first mortgage at 80% LTV, a 10% gift, and a 10% down payment from savings
options.c: A first mortgage at 90% LTV and a 10% down payment, with PMI until 80% LTV
options.d: A first mortgage at 80% LTV, a second lien at 10%, and a 10% down payment

distractorExplanations.a: The structure avoids PMI by using a 10% second lien; it does not involve 10% mortgage insurance coverage.
distractorExplanations.b: An 80-10-10 includes a 10% second mortgage, not a gift; gift-plus-savings would be a 20% down payment.
distractorExplanations.c: A 90% first lien with PMI is a standard conventional loan; the piggyback splits financing into 80% and 10% liens.

options.a: Reduces documentation when replacing an existing FHA/VA loan with a new FHA/VA loan
options.b: Allows cash-out up to 85% of value with reduced income and appraisal documentation
options.c: Converts an FHA loan to a conventional loan without a new appraisal or credit check
options.d: Reduces documentation when refinancing a conventional loan into a new FHA loan

distractorExplanations.b: Streamlines are rate/term refinances with little or no cash back; cash-out refinances require full underwriting and appraisal.
distractorExplanations.c: A streamline must refinance FHA into FHA (or VA into VA via IRRRL); moving to conventional requires full underwriting.
distractorExplanations.d: Conventional-to-FHA refinances require full documentation; streamlines are limited to existing FHA or VA loans.

mortgage-loan-originator-readiness-check.explanation: Streamlines have program-specific eligibility, NTB, and funding fee/MIP rules; the new loan must meet net tangible benefit tests.

options.a: Condo units cannot be financed with any loan that carries private mortgage insurance
options.b: Investor concentration, litigation, or commercial space may exceed agency limits
options.c: TRID requires a separate condo disclosure in place of the Loan Estimate
options.d: The borrower's DTI exceeds 50%, making the condo unit ineligible for agency sale

distractorExplanations.a: Warrantable condos can carry PMI; non-warrantable status comes from project-level issues like litigation or investor concentration.
distractorExplanations.c: TRID has no condo-specific disclosure replacing the LE; project eligibility is set by agency condo guidelines.
distractorExplanations.d: Warrantability is a project-level determination; a borrower's DTI affects the loan, not the condo project's status.

options.a: Exceed the higher area limits for high-cost counties but remain eligible for GSE purchase
options.b: Fall below the baseline conforming limit but carry a higher LTV than standard loans
options.c: Exceed the national baseline conforming limit but remain within higher area limits
options.d: Exceed the FHA county limit and are insured by FHA under its high-cost area program

distractorExplanations.a: Loans above the high-cost area limit are jumbo and not GSE-eligible; high-balance loans stay within the higher area limit.
distractorExplanations.b: Loans under the baseline are standard conforming; high-balance refers to amounts above the baseline in high-cost areas.
distractorExplanations.d: High-balance conforming loans are conventional Fannie/Freddie loans, not FHA-insured; FHA has its own county limits.

options.a: Provide monthly payments to an older homeowner, repaid from sale proceeds when they leave
options.b: Provide a lower interest rate in exchange for the lender's right to call the loan early
options.c: Provide funds as a second lien that accrues interest monthly at a fixed rate
options.d: Provide funds to the homeowner in exchange for a future share of home price appreciation

distractorExplanations.a: Monthly payouts repaid on move-out describe a reverse mortgage (HECM), not a share of future appreciation.
distractorExplanations.b: A call option for a lower rate is a callable loan feature; shared appreciation trades funding for a share of future value.
distractorExplanations.c: A fixed-rate interest-bearing second lien is a home equity loan; equity-sharing repayment is tied to future appreciation.

options.a: Charges interest without reducing principal during the IO period
options.b: Charges less than the full interest, so the unpaid interest is added to principal
options.c: Lets the borrower skip payments during the IO period without accruing interest
options.d: Reduces principal gradually from the first payment, like a standard 30-year loan

distractorExplanations.b: Adding unpaid interest to principal is negative amortization; an IO payment covers the full interest so the balance stays level.
distractorExplanations.c: Interest accrues and must be paid monthly during the IO period; only principal reduction is deferred, not interest.
distractorExplanations.d: Gradual principal reduction from the first payment describes a fully amortizing loan, not the IO period.

mortgage-loan-originator-readiness-check.explanation: IO loans defer principal; after the IO period, amortizing payments typically rise. Payment shock at recast and ATR analysis of the fully amortizing payment are core MLO disclosures.

options.a: Income is taken from the borrower's stated figure without any third-party verification
options.b: Income is inferred from deposits rather than traditional W-2/ tax return verification
options.c: Income is verified with W-2s and tax returns, but assets are not checked at all
options.d: Income is calculated from the property's rent, without any personal income review

distractorExplanations.a: Bank statement loans still verify income through 12-24 months of statements; stated-income lending violates ATR.
distractorExplanations.c: Bank statement programs serve borrowers who lack traditional W-2/tax return income; asset review is still part of underwriting.
distractorExplanations.d: Using property rent to qualify describes a DSCR investor loan, not a bank-statement program based on deposits.

mortgage-loan-originator-readiness-check.explanation: Non-QM bank statement loans need robust deposit analysis, expense factors, and ATR documentation, which is why lenders apply strong overlays.

options.a: Charging more than three points and fees on a Qualified Mortgage
options.b: A seller requiring the buyer to use a particular title insurance company
options.c: Escrow cushions larger than two months of annual escrow disbursements
options.d: Kickbacks and unearned fees tied to settlement service referrals

distractorExplanations.a: The 3% points-and-fees cap is a Reg Z QM requirement, not a RESPA Section 8 prohibition on kickbacks.
distractorExplanations.b: Seller-required title insurance companies are prohibited by RESPA Section 9, not Section 8's kickback rule.
distractorExplanations.c: The two-month (one-sixth) escrow cushion limit is in RESPA Section 10, not Section 8's anti-kickback rule.

options.a: Three business days to cancel after closing disclosures and note signing
options.b: Three calendar days to cancel after funding, including Sundays and holidays
options.c: Three business days to cancel a purchase-money loan on a primary residence
options.d: Seven business days to cancel after the Loan Estimate is delivered

distractorExplanations.b: Rescission runs three business days (Saturdays count, Sundays and federal holidays do not) from consummation, notice, or disclosures, whichever is last.
distractorExplanations.c: Purchase-money (residential mortgage transaction) loans are exempt from rescission; it applies to certain refinances and home equity loans.
distractorExplanations.d: Seven business days is the LE waiting period before consummation, not the post-closing rescission window.

options.a: A copy of the credit report used, with the bureau's contact details only
options.b: An adverse action notice with specific reasons or instructions to obtain reasons
options.c: A written notice within 60 days of the decision stating that the application was denied
options.d: A general statement that the applicant did not meet internal standards

distractorExplanations.a: FCRA requires bureau contact and score disclosure, but ECOA requires an adverse action notice with specific reasons.
distractorExplanations.c: Reg B requires notice within 30 days of a completed application, and it must give or offer the specific reasons.
distractorExplanations.d: Reg B says vague statements like 'failed internal standards' are insufficient; specific principal reasons are required.

options.a: A permissible purpose, plus FCRA notice to the consumer after funding
options.b: Written authorization from the consumer, renewed every 90 days
options.c: A permissible purpose and often written authorization from the consumer
options.d: A HMDA disclosure and adverse action notice before the pull

distractorExplanations.a: The permissible purpose must exist before the pull; FCRA does not make a post-funding notice the authorization.
distractorExplanations.b: FCRA has no 90-day renewal rule; the consumer's credit application itself creates the permissible purpose.
distractorExplanations.d: HMDA disclosures and adverse action notices are unrelated to accessing credit reports; FCRA requires a permissible purpose.

options.a: Race, color, religion, national origin, sex, handicap, and familial status as listed under fair lending law
options.b: Race, color, religion, sex, marital status, age, and the applicant's length of employment or job type
options.c: Race, color, religion, national origin, sex, and age, but not marital status or receipt of public assistance
options.d: Race, color, religion, national origin, sex, marital status, age (with exceptions), receipt of public assistance

distractorExplanations.a: Handicap and familial status are Fair Housing Act bases; ECOA covers marital status, age, and public assistance instead.
distractorExplanations.b: Length of employment is a legitimate underwriting factor, not an ECOA prohibited basis.
distractorExplanations.c: Reg B expressly protects marital status and income from public assistance programs; creditors may not exclude them as prohibited bases.

mortgage-loan-originator-readiness-check.explanation: Protected classes under ECOA and FHA guide fair lending compliance. ECOA also protects good-faith exercise of rights under consumer credit laws.

options.a: Events like interest rate locks after LE issuance or appraisal-driven value changes
options.b: Fee increases the lender documents internally, even when no new information has come to light
options.c: Borrower complaints about fees, which reset all tolerances once a new LE is sent
options.d: Any event discovered after the Closing Disclosure is issued, up to 60 days later

distractorExplanations.b: A changed circumstance needs an extraordinary event, new information, or inaccurate information relied on, not internal paperwork.
distractorExplanations.c: Complaints are not changed circumstances; a revised LE resets baselines only when a valid trigger exists and is sent within 3 business days.
distractorExplanations.d: Changed circumstances justify a revised LE before the CD; the 60-day window applies to post-consummation tolerance refunds.

options.a: An automated valuation model, with the result given to the borrower at closing
options.b: A verbal value estimate from the appraiser before the lender orders the report
options.c: A written appraisal and delivery to the borrower before closing
options.d: A desktop appraisal without interior inspection, shared on borrower request

distractorExplanations.a: HPML rules require a written appraisal with an interior inspection by a certified or licensed appraiser, not an AVM.
distractorExplanations.b: HPML appraisals must be written, and copies delivered at least three business days before consummation.
distractorExplanations.d: HPML rules require a physical interior inspection, and the copy must be provided free without waiting for a request.

mortgage-loan-originator-readiness-check.explanation: Borrowers receive copies and may obtain additional appraisal under certain conditions; this applies to many higher-priced first-lien mortgages.

options.a: Verify each borrower's identity and screen loan applicants against OFAC sanctions lists
options.b: Set annual conforming loan limits based on reported home prices in each county
options.c: Track MLO licensing status and continuing education through annual NMLS filings
options.d: Monitor fair lending patterns and market activity by collecting application and loan data

distractorExplanations.a: Identity verification and OFAC screening are BSA/AML and sanctions duties, not HMDA's data-reporting purpose.
distractorExplanations.b: Conforming limits are set by FHFA using its house price index, not from HMDA LAR data.
distractorExplanations.c: Licensing and CE tracking happen in NMLS under the SAFE Act; HMDA collects application and loan data.

options.a: Provide applicants copies of appraisals and written valuations
options.b: Provide copies of appraisals only if the applicant requests them in writing
options.c: Provide copies of appraisals for loans that close, but not for denied applications
options.d: Provide copies of appraisals after charging the applicant a separate copy fee

distractorExplanations.b: Since 2014, Reg B requires creditors to provide copies promptly without a request; a written request is no longer needed.
distractorExplanations.c: Copies are due promptly or three business days before consummation, and also when the application is denied or withdrawn.
distractorExplanations.d: Reg B bars charging for the copy itself, although a reasonable fee for the appraisal may be charged.

mortgage-loan-originator-readiness-check.explanation: Applicants may review valuations promptly even if credit is denied; the rule covers appraisals and written valuations developed in connection with the application.

options.a: Whether the loan's points and fees fall under the 3% cap that applies to every QM
options.b: How much legal protection the creditor receives if the borrower later challenges ATR compliance
options.c: Whether the creditor must verify the borrower's income and assets before the loan is consummated
options.d: Whether the loan may include negative amortization, interest-only, or balloon payment features

distractorExplanations.a: The 3% points-and-fees cap applies to both safe harbor and rebuttable QMs; the split depends on APR vs APOR pricing.
distractorExplanations.c: Verification is required for QMs and non-QMs alike; safe harbor vs rebuttable presumption concerns litigation protection.
distractorExplanations.d: No QM of either type may have negative amortization or IO features (balloons only in narrow small-creditor cases); that is not the distinction between them.

options.a: At least one business day before consummation, as with the old HUD-1
options.b: At the closing table, together with the note and the security instrument
options.c: At least three business days before consummation
options.d: At least seven business days before consummation, the same as the LE

distractorExplanations.a: The one-day pre-closing review was a HUD-1 rule under old RESPA; the CD must be received three business days before.
distractorExplanations.b: Receipt at the closing table is too late; TRID requires CD receipt at least three business days before consummation.
distractorExplanations.d: Seven business days is the waiting period after LE delivery; the CD rule is three business days before consummation.

mortgage-loan-originator-readiness-check.explanation: Three-day CD rule helps borrowers compare final terms to the Loan Estimate; limited redisclosure rules apply if certain changes occur.

options.a: Remove accurate negative items older than two years by filing a written dispute
options.b: Block lenders from pulling their credit while a dispute is pending with a bureau
options.c: Have the lender correct the credit report directly during underwriting
options.d: Challenge inaccurate credit report information with bureaus and data furnishers

distractorExplanations.a: Accurate negative information can be reported for seven years (bankruptcies up to ten); disputes address inaccuracy.
distractorExplanations.b: A pending dispute does not bar permissible-purpose pulls; it obligates the bureau to investigate, usually within 30 days.
distractorExplanations.c: Lenders cannot alter bureau files; corrections come from bureau and furnisher investigations or a rapid rescore based on them.

options.a: Income/assets, employment, monthly payment, simultaneous mortgage obligations, other debt, DTI/residual, and credit history
options.b: Income/assets, employment, credit history, the property's appraised value, expected appreciation, and the LTV ratio
options.c: Income/assets, employment, monthly payment, and DTI, with credit history excluded under ECOA to prevent discrimination
options.d: Income/assets, employment, other debt, DTI, and credit history, with the monthly payment measured at the introductory teaser rate

distractorExplanations.b: Appreciation forecasts and LTV are collateral considerations; ATR's eight factors focus on the borrower's capacity to repay.
distractorExplanations.c: Credit history is one of the eight ATR factors; ECOA does not bar considering it as a legitimate underwriting factor.
distractorExplanations.d: ATR requires the payment at the fully indexed rate (or the maximum in the first five years), not the introductory teaser rate.

options.a: A second appraisal on every HPML refinance, ordered by the lender at the borrower's expense
options.b: An escrow account for property taxes and insurance for a minimum period after consummation
options.c: Private mortgage insurance for at least five years after consummation, even below 80% LTV
options.d: An escrow account for taxes and insurance that the borrower may cancel after 12 months

distractorExplanations.a: A second appraisal applies to certain HPML flips, not every refinance, and the borrower cannot be charged for it.
distractorExplanations.c: HPML rules require escrow for at least five years; they do not mandate private mortgage insurance.
distractorExplanations.d: HPML escrows generally must be kept at least five years, and cancellation requires LTV under 80% and no delinquency.

options.a: Annual completion of 8 hours of CE, with no federal law or ethics content required
options.b: Completion of 20 hours of CE every two years, focused on nontraditional lending
options.c: Retaking the national test every three years instead of completing annual CE
options.d: Annual completion of federal and state CE including ethics and federal law components

distractorExplanations.a: The 8 annual hours must include 3 hours of federal law, 2 of ethics, and 2 on nontraditional lending.
distractorExplanations.b: Twenty hours is the pre-licensing education minimum; SAFE CE is at least 8 hours every year, not biennial.
distractorExplanations.c: The national test must be retaken only after a licensing lapse of five years or more; CE is the annual requirement.

options.a: Disclosed on loan documents and marketing as required by state and federal rules
options.b: Disclosed on the loan application, but omitted from advertising to avoid confusion
options.c: Disclosed to the borrower verbally at application, with no written disclosure needed
options.d: Shared with the processor so loans can be submitted under the MLO's identifier

distractorExplanations.b: Reg Z and state rules require the NMLS ID on key loan documents, and states generally require it in advertising too.
distractorExplanations.c: Reg Z requires the NMLS ID in writing on the application, note, and security instrument, not just verbally.
distractorExplanations.d: The NMLS ID belongs to the individual MLO; letting others originate under it is unlicensed activity.

options.a: Showing the lowest rate available to top-tier borrowers, with the APR placed in a footnote
options.b: Representing terms actually available to typical qualified applicants with required disclosures
options.c: Listing the monthly payment and rate, with trigger-term disclosures offered upon request
options.d: Advertising a fixed rate that later converts to an adjustable rate, with the change disclosed only after application

distractorExplanations.a: Reg Z requires the APR with equal prominence when a rate is stated, and rates must be reasonably available, not top-tier.
distractorExplanations.c: Payment amounts are trigger terms, so required disclosures must appear in the ad itself, not on request.
distractorExplanations.d: Ads must clearly disclose rate changes; hiding an ARM conversion until after application is misleading.

options.a: RESPA Section 8 rules prohibiting referral fees between the MLO and the borrower
options.b: HMDA rules requiring the MLO to report the higher-cost loan to regulators as a steering violation
options.c: Fair lending and LO compensation rules prohibiting predatory steering for personal gain
options.d: SAFE Act rules capping MLO commissions at a fixed percentage of the loan amount

distractorExplanations.a: Section 8 targets kickbacks among settlement providers; steering for higher pay is addressed by LO comp and fair lending rules.
distractorExplanations.b: HMDA collects pricing data for analysis; it does not classify individual loans as steering violations.
distractorExplanations.d: The SAFE Act governs licensing and does not cap commissions; steering is governed by Reg Z anti-steering rules.

options.a: A Good Faith Estimate early and a HUD-1 settlement statement one day before closing
options.b: The Closing Disclosure early, with the Loan Estimate delivered at the closing table
options.c: The Loan Estimate early, with the Closing Disclosure delivered after funding
options.d: TRID disclosures including the Loan Estimate early and Closing Disclosure before closing

distractorExplanations.a: The GFE and HUD-1 were replaced by the LE and CD for most closed-end mortgages in October 2015.
distractorExplanations.b: The order is reversed: the LE comes within 3 business days of application and the CD at least 3 business days before closing.
distractorExplanations.c: The CD must be received before consummation, at least three business days ahead, not after funding.

options.a: A timely AfBA disclosure of the relationship and estimated charges
options.b: An AfBA disclosure, after which the borrower may be required to use the affiliate
options.c: A verbal mention of the affiliation at closing, with the charges shown on the CD
options.d: A disclosure of the relationship, with referral fees paid to the MLO per closed file

distractorExplanations.b: Disclosure does not authorize mandatory use; RESPA generally bars requiring an affiliated title company as a condition.
distractorExplanations.c: The AfBA disclosure must be written and given at or before the referral, not verbally at closing.
distractorExplanations.d: AfBA compliance allows ownership returns, not per-referral payments; fees for referrals remain Section 8 kickbacks.

mortgage-loan-originator-readiness-check.explanation: AfBA disclosures explain the relationship and charges; RESPA still generally bars requiring a particular title company, so disclosure is not a license to require it.

options.a: Paying originators a fixed percentage of the loan amount on each closed loan
options.b: Varying originator compensation based on loan terms or conditions
options.c: Paying originators more for higher loan volume or a larger number of closings
options.d: Reducing originator compensation to cover an unforeseen closing cost increase

distractorExplanations.a: A fixed percentage of the loan amount is permitted (with small-loan limits); the ban is on comp that varies with loan terms.
distractorExplanations.c: Volume-based compensation is permitted because volume is not a loan term; terms such as rate or fees cannot drive pay.
distractorExplanations.d: Reg Z allows an originator to reduce comp to cover unforeseen increases in third-party settlement costs.

options.a: Share the contract price and target value so the appraiser can confirm it
